To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a space-based instrument with 2×2-km2 spatial resolution and 0.5%-precision can be used to detect and quantify CO2 emissions from individual power plants.

(1) strong localized point sources such as power plants (PP) can be detected and quantified from space with a precision of better than 1.5% (6 MtCO2/PP) and (2) the proposed concept has the potential of contributing to an independent verification system of global CO2 emissions.
In summary, our research is concerned with

developing a satellite instrument concept for a future generation satellite mission which can contribute to the detection and monitoring of anthropogenic GHG emissions and to global regional-scale CO 2 and CH 4 surface flux inverse modelling.
a new satellite remote sensing technique which will provide unprecedented global coverage of the distribution of CO2 and CH 4 and their isotopologues.
a satellite mission concept for global monitoring of anthropogenic CO2 emission sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a satellite concept for global CO2 monitoring is feasible and that it has the potential to provide important new information for a variety of applications.
a satellite instrument based on the concept described in this paper is capable of measuring the CO2 emissions from power plants with a precision of a few percent.
the investigated concept can be used for global monitoring of anthropogenic CO2 emission from space and is also useful in a variety of other applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an operational satellite remote sensing instrument concept that is capable of monitoring the CO2 emissions from all major power plants on Earth.

a single satellite with a 500 km swath can provide a 6-day revisit time for the entire globe, which allows to monitor anthropogenic CO2 emission at a precision of 1.5 MtCO 2/yr (2.5%) and a spatial resolution of better than 2×2 kilometers.

a single satellite instrument with the discussed characteristics can be used to monitor the global distribution of CO2, CH4, N2O and other GHGs, to quantify their surface fluxes and to quantify emissions from strong point sources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the concept for global monitoring of strong CO2 point sources is feasible with existing or soon-to-be-available technologies.

a single satellite with an appropriate instrument can deliver the data needed to monitor a large variety of anthropogenic CO2 emitters, including power plants and large cities, with a precision of a few percent.
a global anthropogenic CO2 emission monitoring system is feasible with existing technology.
